metinler: The profession that puts out fires, rescues people in accidents, earthquakes and floods, and educates the public to prevent fires: from recruit to station commander.
Heat, smoke, heights and confined spaces
Heavy equipment, strict discipline and teamwork

This certificate shows the training content completed in the Meslektaş game; it is not an official certificate and does not authorise you to respond to fires. In Türkiye, becoming a firefighter requires the conditions in municipalities' recruitment notices (education, KPSS exam, driving licence, physical fitness). In a real fire, call 112 first.
Civil Defence and Firefighting course content from MEB and universities (in our own words)
TS EN 2 fire classes; class F (cooking oils) is defined in EN 3-7
Regulation on the Protection of Buildings from Fire (Türkiye)
Municipal Fire Brigade Regulation and firefighter recruitment notices (checked in October 2026, Türkiye)
Basic life support values: current European Resuscitation Council guidelines
Air, water and ladder calculations are examples for training purposes
At Recruit level you'll learn how fire starts, the equipment and how to use an extinguisher.
A day in the life of a firefighter
A firefighter puts out fires and rescues people in incidents such as traffic accidents, earthquakes, floods and people trapped in lifts.
Fire stations are open day and night. Crews work shifts; when the alarm comes, they're on the road within minutes.
At the start of the shift, the vehicle, hoses, breathing sets and rescue tools are checked one by one.
A firefighter trains and drills every day. Working with heavy equipment takes strength and stamina.
In Türkiye, the single emergency number for fire, health and security is 112.

In Türkiye, municipalities recruit firefighters through public notices. Usually a graduate degree from a firefighting or civil defence associate programme, a KPSS score, a driving licence and physical fitness are required; the conditions vary by notice.
You're on an introduction day at a fire station. A firefighter is showing you around.
The alarm went off. The crew is running to the vehicle.
I clear the way and wait where I was told, without getting in anyone's way
In an alarm every second counts. Someone untrained mustn't get in the crew's way.
I'll get in the vehicle too
An untrained person doesn't go to the scene.
I grab the equipment and help
Everything has its set place and order; it mustn't be mixed up.
Firefighter: "What do you think the first rule in a fire is?"
Safety of life first: people and the crew itself
Property can be saved or bought again; a life doesn't come back.
Belongings come after the safety of life.
At the scene, duty comes first.
You're curious about the firefighting suit hanging up and want to touch it.
I ask permission; I don't disturb where the equipment is or how it's arranged
The suit and equipment are arranged to be put on in seconds.
I'll try it on and put it back
If the arrangement is disturbed, time is lost in an alarm.
In an alarm, clear the way and don't get in the crew's way.
The arrangement of equipment isn't disturbed.
There are no right or wrong answers. Choose the one closest to you.
Physically demanding work with heavy equipment?
It would be hard for me
Waking up in the middle of the night and rushing straight to work?
I could get used to it
It would be hard for me
Staying calm in a frightening situation?
Working as a team, following the rules exactly?
Working at heights or in confined spaces?
You're strong and cool-headed. The station is waiting; go on to Recruit level!
Some aspects suit you. Play the Recruit level to get to know the profession up close.
The physical pace and danger may be challenging for you. Fire safety consulting or first aid training might interest you.
Firefighter level unlocked: building fires, CPR and incidents in the field.
Burning needs three things: fuel, heat and oxygen. If one is removed, the fire goes out.
Substances such as water put fire out by lowering the heat.
Foam, a blanket, a lid or carbon dioxide put fire out by cutting off its contact with air.
Moving the fuel away from the flame or closing the gas valve also puts the fire out.
A: solids (wood, paper). B: liquids (petrol, paint). C: gases (LPG, natural gas). D: metals (magnesium). Cooking oil fires are referred to separately as class F.
Most deaths in fires are caused by smoke, not flames. Smoke carries toxic gases and fills a room in the blink of an eye.
A heat-resistant suit, helmet, hood, gloves and boots protect the firefighter from flames and heat.
A breathing set with a clean-air cylinder carried on the back makes it possible to breathe in smoke. The air is limited; the time is monitored.
There are dry chemical powder (ABC), carbon dioxide, foam and water extinguishers. The label on it says which class it's suitable for.
The pump on the vehicle pushes water into the hoses. The nozzle can deliver water as a straight jet or as a fog (spray).
Portable ladders and ladder vehicles make it possible to reach heights and carry out rescues.
Hydraulic cutters and spreaders are used to get a person trapped in an accident out of a vehicle.
Put each burning material in its fire class.
A metal fire is class D and needs a special powder.
Hot cooking oil in a pan
Water is never poured on a cooking oil (F) fire.
A solid, B liquid, C gas, D metal.
Cooking oil fires are referred to separately as class F.
The first step when using a fire extinguisher?
The trigger doesn't work until the pin is pulled.
At the top of the flames
At the base of the flames, at the burning material
A fire is put out where the burning material is.
When using an extinguisher, where should the exit be?
If you can't control it, you must be able to retreat immediately.
In which classes is a dry powder (ABC) extinguisher used?
The letters on its label show this.
Where should the needle on the pressure gauge be?
Pull the pin → aim the hose at the base of the flames → squeeze the trigger → sweep to put it out.
The needle should be in the green.
As a recruit, you're taking part in a fire drill at a school.
As the students leave, a group heads for the lift.
I tell them not to use the lift and direct them to the stairs
In a fire, a lift can stop or fill with smoke.
The lift is fast, let them use it
A lift is dangerous in a fire.
A drill is for teaching the right behaviour.
A teacher wants to go back to get the bags in the classroom.
I tell them not to go back, that lives matter, not belongings
In a real fire, going back is one of the most common causes of death.
Within seconds smoke can block the way.
You'd put two people in danger.
Everyone is at the assembly point. What's next?
I make sure a head count is done with the class lists
If someone is missing, they may still be inside; the first job is the head count.
A head count is done first.
Everyone goes back into the building
Nobody goes back until the drill is over.
Lifts aren't used in a fire.
A head count is done at the assembly point.
Put out a fire with an extinguisher
Cardboard has started burning in a storeroom, and the fire is still small. Do the steps in the right order.
A fire that looks small can grow within minutes; help is called immediately.
Choose the extinguisher suited to the fire's class, make sure your escape route is behind you
The wrong extinguisher can make a fire bigger; the exit should be behind you, not in front.
Help has been called; know the fire and the exit.
The trigger doesn't work until the pin is pulled.
The extinguisher is in your hand; first move?
Aim the hose at the base of the flames, at the burning material
Powder sprayed at the top of the flames is wasted.
The pin is pulled; where will you aim?
Squeeze the trigger and sweep from side to side to put it out
The sweeping motion covers the whole burning surface.
You've aimed; now put it out.
Watch for re-ignition, ventilate the area, inform the crew
Cardboard that seems out can keep smouldering inside.
No flames are visible; is it over?
Alarm and 112 → class and exit → pin → base of the flames → squeeze and sweep → watch.
If the fire is big, don't try to put it out: get out and close the door.
The parts of the fire triangle?
If one is removed, the fire goes out.
Which class is a petrol fire?
Which class is an LPG fire?
The first step with an extinguisher?
At the top of the flames
At the base of the flames
What causes most deaths in fires?
Sergeant level unlocked: flashover, air management and search.
Before opening a closed door, its heat is checked with the back of the hand. If it's hot, there's fire behind it; the door is opened in a controlled way, standing to the side.
Hot smoke collects higher up. In smoke, you move low down.
A firefighter never enters a smoke-filled building alone. They go in with their partner and come out with them.
When visibility drops to zero, following the wall keeps you from losing your way.
A firefighter can give basic life support to someone they rescue until the medical team arrives.
Before intervening, the building's electricity and gas are cut off if possible.
The gauge is rising. Press STOP when it reaches the right value. The values follow current first aid guidelines for adults.
The correct depth is about 5–6 cm.
Too deep; the risk of injury increased.
Not deep enough; blood isn't being pumped well enough.
Too fast; the heart doesn't have time to fill.
Use an automated external defibrillator (AED) if available.
Put each fire in the right group.
A class A fire; water cools it.
It's put out with water, and the surroundings are soaked.
Hot oil burning in a pan
Water instantly turns to steam and splashes burning oil everywhere.
Water conducts electricity; the power is cut off first.
A metal fire such as magnesium
Water can make a metal fire more violent.
A straight water jet on petrol spread on the ground
Petrol floats on water and the fire spreads; foam is used.
Hot oil: a lid or fire blanket.
You're now a firefighter who goes out in the field. Three different calls came in today.
There's a strong smell of natural gas in an apartment building. A neighbour is about to switch on a light.
I tell them not to touch the light or any electrical switch, and we close the valve and ventilate
Even a small spark from a switch can cause an explosion. In Türkiye, the natural gas emergency line 187 is also called.
If they switch on the light, we'll see the leak better
We find the leak with a lighter
An open flame is never used.
In a restaurant, oil in a pan caught fire, and the cook is running with a bucket of water.
I stop them; we turn off the stove and cover the pan with a lid or fire blanket
Hot oil that comes into contact with water splashes as if it's exploding.
Let them pour water, it goes out fast
Water makes an oil fire bigger.
Burning oil can spill while being carried.
Smoke and sparks are coming from a shop's electrical panel.
First I cut the power, then use a carbon dioxide or dry powder extinguisher
In an electrical fire, water conducts; the power is cut off first.
I spray water with the hose
I close the panel by hand
Gas smell: don't touch switches, close the valve, ventilate (187 in Türkiye).
Oil fire: no water, smother it by covering.
It's smothered with a lid or blanket
Water is never poured on it.
Switches aren't touched, the valve is closed
There may be fire behind it; it's opened in a controlled way from the side
It's checked with the back of the hand.
You go in with your partner
You go in without breathing apparatus
Station commander level unlocked: incident management, priorities and crew health.
In a closed room, as the temperature rises, everything can ignite at the same time. Dense hot smoke at the ceiling and flames rolling across the ceiling are warning signs.
If air suddenly enters a closed fire that's low on oxygen, an explosion-like flare-up can happen. A closed space isn't opened in an uncontrolled way.
The air in a breathing set is limited. The crew plans so that when air runs low, enough is left for the way back.
On the radio, you speak briefly, clearly and in turn. An emergency call takes precedence over everything.
In buildings that have burned for a long time, ceilings and floors can collapse. Cracks, sagging and strange noises are watched for.
The sergeant leads their crew at the scene: deciding who goes in where and when they come out.
Match each sign to the right danger.
A very hot smoke layer rapidly thickening under the ceiling
The heat is bringing everything in the room to ignition temperature.
Tongues of flame rolling through the smoke at the ceiling
Gases have started burning at the ceiling.
Smoke coming from furniture on its own
The furniture is about to ignite.
The windows of a closed room blackened with soot
The fire may have run out of oxygen.
Smoke being drawn in at a door gap and pushed out again
The fire is looking for air.
The door is very hot, with few flames visible inside
It's very hot inside but low on oxygen.
A whistling sound from door gaps
Flashover: thick hot smoke at the ceiling, rolling flames, unbearable heat.
Backdraft: sooty windows, breathing smoke, a hot door, a whistling sound.
When in doubt, pull back and tell the commander.
A breathing set has 1,600 L of usable air, and 50 L per minute is used during heavy work. About how many minutes?
1,600 ÷ 50 = 32 minutes. In reality, a margin is left for the way back.
A common training rule: one third of the air for going in, one third for coming back, one third in reserve. With 1,800 L, at most how much for going in?
The vehicle's tank holds 3,000 L of water, and the hose delivers 300 L per minute. How many minutes will the water last?
3,000 ÷ 300 = 10 minutes; connect to a hydrant early.
A common ladder rule: the foot's distance from the wall is a quarter of the height. For 8 m?
Two hoses each deliver 250 litres per minute. The total?
Air time = air ÷ consumption per minute.
Ladder foot ≈ a quarter of the height.
It's been reported that someone may be inside. You'll search a smoke-filled flat with your crew. Do the steps in the right order.
Pair up with your partner, check your breathing set's air and the radio
You don't go in with low air or a radio that doesn't work.
Check the door's heat with the back of your hand before opening it, stand to the side
This is how the danger behind the door is understood.
Go in low, follow a wall
Hot smoke is up high; the wall keeps you from getting lost.
Search the rooms systematically: under beds, wardrobes, bathroom; mark each searched room
People hide when they're scared; the same room isn't searched twice.
You're inside; where will you look?
Take the person you found out through the nearest safe exit and hand them over to the medical team
The rescued person needs medical help immediately.
Report the search result and your remaining air to the crew commander
The commander must know which area has been searched.
Partner and equipment → door check → enter low, follow the wall → systematic search → removal → report.
As a fire sergeant, you lead a crew.
Someone may be trapped inside, but flames are seen rolling across the ceiling of the room.
I pull the crew back, cool the ceiling with water, and continue the search once conditions improve
In a flashover, you could lose the crew too. The environment is brought under control first.
Going in while there are flashover signs could kill the crew.
A young firefighter says "let me check one more room" even though the low-air alarm has gone off.
I order them to come out immediately and send a crew with full air in their place
If the air runs out, the rescuer also becomes someone who needs rescuing.
I praise their courage and let them carry on
I give them my own air
That puts two people in danger.
Someone at the scene wants to photograph the injured and share the pictures.
I make sure they're moved outside the safety cordon and protect the privacy of the injured
Images of victims are the right of the victims and their families.
Let them share it, it'll make the news
At flashover signs, pull back and cool.
At the low-air alarm, you come out.
The privacy of victims is protected.
What are flames rolling across the ceiling a sign of?
Windows blackened with soot and breathing smoke?
1,500 L of air, 50 L per minute consumption?
The ladder foot at a height of 12 m is about?
So that the same room isn't searched twice during a search?
The air for the way back is protected.
At the end of a search?
The result and remaining air are reported to the commander
How do you move in a smoke-filled area?
You've completed the whole path from recruit to station commander!
In a big incident, one person takes command, assigns tasks and coordinates with other agencies (health, police, AFAD in Türkiye).
First the safety of life, then bringing the incident under control and preventing it from spreading, and protecting property last.
In long incidents, crews are rested, and their drinking water and medical checks are ensured.
Fire inspections in buildings, public education and drills prevent fires from the start.
After every incident, what went well and what should be improved is discussed and a report is written.
Serious incidents affect firefighters too. Talking and getting support isn't weakness; it's part of the profession.
Give each task the right priority.
Tracking the crews' air and positions
The crew are lives that must be protected too.
Handing an injured person over to the medical team
Preventing spread to the neighbouring building with a water curtain
The fire is kept from growing.
Cutting off the building's gas and electricity
Moving chemical drums away from the fire
After life safety and control are ensured.
Moving valuable documents to a safe place
2. Controlling the incident and preventing spread.
24 firefighters at the station are to be split equally into 3 shifts. Per shift?
At an incident, 4 crews each work 45 minutes and then go to rest. The total crew working time?
The station responded to 1,200 calls a year. The monthly average?
The target: arrive within 10 minutes for 90% of calls. For how many of 200 calls?
Last year 80 fires, this year 60. By what percentage did they fall?
20 ÷ 80 = 25%. Prevention work may be paying off.
Resources are split evenly across shifts.
The arrival time target is monitored.
Rate of change = difference ÷ old value.
As station commander, you're in command of a major incident.
Two big calls came in at the same time, and only one crew is free at the station.
I send the crew to the one with the higher risk to life and immediately ask neighbouring stations for support
When resources aren't enough, priority is given by risk to life and support is called.
I choose the first one that came in
I split the crew in two and send it to both
An undermanned crew may fail at both.
The crews have been working for 3 hours, and one complains of dizziness.
I take them for rest and a health check and put in a fresh crew in their place
A tired firefighter has accidents; the crew's health is also life safety.
Let them hold out a bit longer
Let them drink some water and carry on
The incident is over, and the crew saw a very distressing scene.
I hold a debriefing talk with the crew and arrange psychological support if needed
If the effects of serious incidents are ignored, they build up.
I tell them you get used to it in this profession
The need for support isn't belittled.
I start them on a new shift right away
When resources fall short, prioritise by risk to life and get support at once.
Support is provided after serious incidents.

The air for the way back is protected.
